# Executive Summary 

###### Over supply on the horizon 

- Our short term view remains similar to January.  Deficits through H1 2013 will drive stocks down to critically low levels and prices will rise towards $10,000/t by Q2 2013.  In the medium term, demand growth has been raised and mine production lowered, meaning that the surpluses forecast from 2014 to 2016 are lower and prices slightly higher. 

- China dominates consumption growth, though in 2012 China is now expected to rise by only 6.3% due to a slow H1.

We expect a bounce in H2, as monetary policy loosening leads to higher output of copper containing end-use products. However, the government’s focus on deflating the property bubble means that construction demand will remain constrained. - In the short term, increases to consumption forecasts for the USA, Brazil and the Middle East, as well as a less negative outlook for Europe, will compensate somewhat for the slower Chinese growth. In 2013, a synchronised cyclical macroeconomic upswing will lift global refined consumption growth to over 5% and an average of over 4% in 2014-16. - In 2011, mine production fell slightly, but higher scrap use at smelters and refineries meant refined output grew by an estimated 2.1%. This year, we expect refined supply growth to be flat, as a modest rise in electrorefined production is offset by a small fall in EW output. The wave of new mine projects remains on course to begin in earnest in 2013 and we forecast 1Mt or higher refined output for each year from 2013 to 2016. - High Chinese imports have seen stocks build there, which we expect will be drawn down over the rest of 2012, feeding the majority of the refined market deficit of over 500,000t that we forecast for this year. This will leave a small stock build in the world ex-China, which combined with a slow return of investor money due to uncertain demand prospects means prices should rise only modestly through the rest of 2012. - With excess Chinese stocks whittled down, the market moving into a 150,000t deficit next year means exchange stocks should fall to low levels in H1 2013 and the price spike towards $10,000/t. Thereafter, mine projects will continue to boost refined supply, tipping the market into surplus. By 2016, a 560,000t increase in stocks will weigh on the price, which we forecast will see an annual average below $7,500/t ($3.40/lb). |Table I: LME Copper price

Refined consumption in 2010-11 in the rest of Asia has been upwardly revised due to stronger wirerod growth in the Middle East. As the result of a higher base in 2011, refined consumption growth in the Middle East is higher throughout the forecast period. US (better economic prospects) and Brazilian (faster growth due to the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics) consumption has also been raised slightly compared to January. Western European growth is also less pessimistic than three months ago but changes to Russian export duties will lower consumption in Eastern Europe from 2014. The net result is global consumption being higher by 170,000t in 2012, 280,000t in 2014 but only 200,000t by 2016. **Supply** : 2011 mine output was less disrupted than we had expected in January, meaning that refined production last year is 370,000t higher than we had estimated. Potential refined production has been lowered by an average of 100,000t/y in the 2012-2016 period. However, higher mine output means that actual refined production is forecast to be an average of 70,000t/y higher than three months ago. **Prices** : Prices for 2012 have been lowered by $350/t and by $200/t in 2013 as a result of a slower decline in stocks to critically low levels. Conversely, a slower move into surplus and build in stocks means the price falls more slowly and is $525/t higher in 2015, with the 560,000t surplus in 2016 leaving the price only $100/t higher that year. ###### Demand uncertainty holds market in check The uncertainty over demand prospects (both up and down) held the copper price in a narrow $8,200-8,600/t range since mid-January 2012 on the LME. The outlook for China over H1 2012 has deteriorated as the credit squeeze to deflate the property bubble means that the productive sector of the economy is still suffering constrained credit availability. In addition, the squeeze on the construction sector is hindering demand for copper from this sector directly plus via demand for domestic appliances and other products which are influenced by increased housing activity. Sustained imports of a combined 711,000t in JanuaryFebruary mean that the outturn for Q1 2012 could again be over 1Mt. The rise in bonded warehouse stocks by an estimated 90,000t in March (300,000t in the quarter) supports our view that imports were sustained in the last month of Q1. This broadly repeats the pattern of last year, when the usual trader restocking ahead of higher demand after the Spring Festival combined with collateral stock imports (mainly by property speculators) to see SHFE and bonded stocks rise to an estimated 732,000t in March 2011. These stocks were then drawn down throughout the year as imports slowed to well below 200,000t/m. The reason for the increase in imports this year is less clear than in 2011. We believe that the Q4 2011 increase was mostly related to traders engaging in their seasonal increase in stocks ahead of the Chinese New Year, which occurred in January instead of February in 2011. They may also have done so to take advantage of the fall in prices in September and October. What is clear is that the high imports in Q1 were not due to property speculators, as the crackdown on the property sector has generally borne fruit and reduced this activity significantly. The analysts in our China office have discover

ed that some traders have been using copper to obtain credit to make plays in other markets.  One is on the arbitrage in the RMB using financial instruments linked to the RMB in Hong Kong and the value of the RMB on the mainland.  In addition, the steady appreciation in the value of the RMB is offering opportunities to speculate in currency movements using Letters of Credit for copper in the RMB and the US$.  Given that China is structurally short of copper, these traders can count on eventually selling the imported material into the country.  Alternatively, metal held in bonded warehouses could be re-exported as long as the SHFE/LME arbitrage window remains firmly closed. 

###### ...but growth expected to draw Shanghai stocks down 

We believe that this game will wind down in Q2.  The consumption outlook for H1 in China is not as buoyant as previously expected.  The build up in stocks to levels above last year will give pause to those using copper as part of a wider trading strategy, as the scope for the market to absorb ever higher stock levels is less than expected.  We therefore anticipate that imports will decline sharply from April. 

As for Chinese copper consumption, it did strengthen seasonally after the New Year, just not as much as market participants had hoped.  In part this is due to a build up in end-use products (such as domestic appliances) that need to be worked down before demand for copper semis can

###### US outlook improves but does not explain LME stock changes 

The USA is the other region where stock developments could have implications for the short term outlook.  We have raised our US consumption forecast based on an improvement in economic prospects.  LME stocks helped supply demand from Q2 2010 to Q3 2011 and are again likely to be the first port of call for traders looking for metal as demand picks up. 

However, higher US demand does not explain the massive increase in cancelled warrants in the country since January.  Cancellations started in New Orleans in December and climbed steadily in large steps to a high of almost 68,000t by the end of January.  At that time the focus shifted to St Louis, where warrant cancellations rose throughout February to reach 40,000t by the beginning of March.  Through 5 April the New Orleans stocks have fallen by about 30,000t and St Louis by just over 23,000t on 31 January levels. 

This rise in US cancellations took total LME cancelled warrants to their highest level since 2004, when the initial boom in copper prices due to the rise of China began.  However, shipments to China do not (yet) explain this development, as imports there from the USA rose only modestly in February (the latest data point available).  An increase in imports from the USA may appear in the March import figures, but the massive negative SHFE/LME arbitrage alone (which averaged $371/t in March 2012) would mean the importer is facing a paper loss of over 4%, not counting transaction costs. 

We believe that the New Orleans withdrawals most likely are for one of two reasons.  It could be warehouse competition, with a large warrant holder moving metal out of the LME system to take advantage of a cheaper storage deal.  Another possibility is a move off warrant of metal by a large financial player, who is taking a bet on the market tightening, as we forecast. With a flat forward curve such, a player could hedge the downside and wait for the price to rise. They would also be in a position to benefit from a tightening of physical availability and higher premia later this year or early in 2013.  Opacity of off warrant stock information makes it extremely difficult to come up with definitive explanations for such movements.  These are two reasons we think could explain such a large move of metal off warrant in such a short time. 

A financial p

layer making a large bet would likely have moved simultaneously on both New Orleans and St Louis. So we tend to believe that the St Louis cancellations are explained by traders who were expecting to use the LME as a source of supply in Q2 jumping in and booking tonnages now, so as not to be caught out. There was a parallel lesser increase in cancellations in Chicago and draw downs from Comex began in early April. Both of these latter stock movements provide supporting evidence that demand is improving in the US, with traders again using the exchanges as their initial source of supply as in 2010-11. ###### Synchronised upswing in consumption in 2013 In 2013, we expect a synchronised cyclical macroeconomic upswing to lift global refined consumption growth to over 5% and then to average over 4% in 2014-16 (see the chart at the top of the following page). Downside macroeconomic and financial risks and their consequent negative impact on consumption are offsetting the upside risks of lower copper production and higher investor inflows into copper. The first is that tight availability of equipment, qualified personnel, water, power, etc. mean that sequencing of projects (at both the company and industry levels) will be a serious challenge. ###### **Macroeconomic and financial risks** 

The key risk to the copper price is the uncertainty of how the global economy will perform. The apparent improvement in the US could prove short-lived and China could possibly not see a return to growth in H2 2012.  The Eurozone crisis could also still prompt more financial market turmoil. 

On the other hand, economic growth in both the US and China could prove stronger than forecast in the base case.  This would be positive for growth in these important consuming countries, but also in those emerging markets which export to these two large economies. 

###### **Consumption risks** 

###### **Downside** 

Aluminium producers are currently facing challenging conditions, with the industry in a situation of chronic oversupply.  Smelter closures have finally begun, with many of the closures directly impacting captive hot metal wirerod plants at aluminium smelters.  So, despite a Cu:Al price ratio of around 3.8:1, supply constraints are likely to prevent aluminium from increasing its market share in the rod sector in the short term.  Longer term though, the substitution threat remains significant for copper demand growth in wirerod.  We expect aluminium will make more inroads into the insulated power cable market as a result of an increase in aluminium wirerod capacity available to target this segment by 2015. 

CRU forecasts that the ratio of the copper price to that of aluminium will average close to 4:1, which will weigh on all consumers’ strategic decision-making.

This is because copper has a range of useful properties which means that it is processed for a wide variety of applications. This means that world IP is a very useful factor for forecasting global copper demand. At a regional/national level, however, the relationship is less reliable due to an often lower diversification in the product type, and number of copper semis fabricators in the area. This means that a broad national/regional industrial production indicator will not be able to highlight what may be significant changes in copper demand due to the national/regional exposure to product-specific trends or company strategy. For example, a strategic decision by a company to upsize a facility to serve export markets might have a dramatic effect on a nation’s copper consumption growth, outperforming the broader change in its industrial production by a large ma

rgin. Despite this limitation on the depth of use that industrial production has in reliably determining copper consumption, there are still many things that may be learnt from the global picture of copper consumption. Furthermore, plotting total copper consumption (cathode and direct-use scrap consumption) alongside the change in global industrial production would theoretically highlight any periods when the market was/will be rationed or where the copper market has grown differently due to a significant new use or through the impact of substitution. ###### 2.3 Points to watch 

- An easing of monetary policy in China during H2 2012 is expected to encourage more refined copper consumption.  This is only likely to occur once the government considers the inflation problem to have been abated.  However, the continued focus on keeping property prices falling may make it difficult to selectively ease credit to other sectors. Local government funding in China had depended on land sales to the commercial property sector.  With these drying up, funding to complete social units may be constrained or diverted.  So, progress on completions of social housing units could be less than assumed in the base case. 

- Copper semis production overcapacity in China.  Although copper semis production is growing, we estimate that the rate of growth in production capacity has been faster.  We believe that utilisation rates in China will remain low during 2012. 

- A materialisation of the gloomy export demand outlook on China’s electronics and appliances manufacturing sectors. The impact of which will depend upon the degree of any downturn in the US and European markets. 

- Weakened threat of substitution of copper with aluminium in 2012.  Due to planned cutbacks to global installed aluminium smelting/fabricating capacity (mainly at integrated aluminium smelters).  This will further tighten the supply of aluminium rod for use in insulated wire and cable, reducing its impact upon refined copper consumption. 

- A quickening of substitution pressures from 2014-15.  As China completes its power infrastructure development, aluminium overhead conductor manufacturing facilities will become available to produce other products.  We believe that insulated wire and cable is the most likely candidate owing to the similarity in processing, thus negatively impacting refined copper consumption. 

- The commercial success of the aluminium wire harness.  Furukawa introduced this new product line to the market only very recently.  The product boasts numerous advantages to copper wire harness, however, automakers might be cautious about using it without a proven track record.

###### **3.1.1 North America** 

Positive events in the USA in the past quarter have led to an upward revision of our forecast for North American refined copper consumption in 2012.  Regional consumption for the full year now stands at 1.96Mt, up from 1.94Mt, which we proposed in the January issue.  This represents a swing in

the growth rate from our previously estimated -0.2% y-o-y to +1.0% y-oy, which is principally attributed to an increased level of copper semis production in the United States as refined copper consumption is now predicted to rise by 1.5% y-o-y to reach 1.6Mt in 2012. 

After flat  growth in the US in 2011, we have witnessed some more promising signs for copper demand in 2012.  The **US Institute of Supply Management** ’s manufacturing PMIs for January and February were 54.1% and 52.4%, indicating market growth.  Furthermore, the copper intensive segments: transport equipment, electrical equipment and fabricated metal products, all registered growing production and orders in January and February after weaker demand seen in Q4 2011. ###### 3.2 Europe ###### **3.2.1 Western Europe** The outlook for Western European copper consumption has improved since the previous issue. PMI data from **HSBC-Markit** indicates that production volumes at European downstream copper users rose by a significant amount after a slight rise in January which followed three consecutive months of contraction. Copper purchases made by semis fabricators, on the other hand, decreased again in February, indicating that semis fabricators reduced raw material stocks. The decline in purchasing activity follows a downward trend which began in July 2011. However, February was the smallest decrease seen in the past 7 months, fuelling hope that European copper purchasing may see positive growth from late Q1 onwards, following the end of a destocking period. The prevailing macroeconomic predictions for 2012 and 2013 in Western Europe, as indicated by industrial production indices, have worsened slightly since the previous issue. However, conditions as reported by copper consumers, while acknowledging the continuing negative impact of the European Debt Crisis, do not suggest an equivalent weakening and there is even some cautious optimism returning for demand from H2 2012 and into 2013. European downstream consumers have been procuring supplies of copper cathode and semis on the spot market after ordering insufficient volumes to meet demand on annual contract alone. ###### **3.2.2 Eastern and Central Europe** 

Following aggregate copper cathode market growth in Eastern European nations of 24% y-o-y in 2011, we expect a further increase in demand of 2.5% y-o-y in 2012, taking the total annual market size to 1.04Mt.  Most of the growth is attributable to Russia increasing wirerod production due to the re-imposition of an export tax on cathode. 

As noted in the January issue, Russia experienced rapid growth in wirerod production following the reintroduction of a copper cathode export duty in January 2011.  Refined copper consumption was also supported by a sustained rise in vehicle sales, which has prompted huge increases in domestic automotive production as carmakers expand facilities to gain a stronger market presence in anticipation of more demand growth.  2012 is set to deliver on more auto sales growth, **LMC-Automotive** forecast sales to rise by 4.1% y-o-y to 2.8M units. 

We do not expect another double-digit percentage rise in Russia wirerod production in 2012 due to our understanding that the structural shift from cathode export to domestic consumption in the form of wirerod production was largely completed in 2011.  Turkey absorbed a lot of the wirerod exports, rising by 122% y-o-y (according to Russian customs) to 62,710t in 2011, which is around 36% greater than the highest annual Turkey-destined export shipment level, achieved in 2007.  Most of the increase that we are forecasting for Russian copper semis production in 2012 is attributed to organic growth in domestic consumption for the production of wire and cable both for its expanding automotive sector and energy cables for the power infrastructure, oil and gas sectors. 

**KGHM** is responsible for most of the re

fined consumption of copper in Poland.  We estimate that in 2011, the company’s production of wirerod of around 226,000t accounted for 86% of Poland’s refined copper consumption.  137,000t of wirerod was exported from Poland in 2011, indicating that 52% of refined copper demand is non-domestic. This foreign demand is almost entirely European-based, with 32% from the Czech Republic, 19% in Germany and 17% in Hungary.  Poland’s refined copper consumption is therefore highly driven by demand from cablemaking manufacturing facilities in Central Europe. 

The **Central Statistical Office** in Poland reported that the initial two months of 2012 had seen a drop of 16.3% y-o-y in insulated cables and conductors.  This may have been as a result of substitution for the use of aluminium cables in infrastructure projects, because the statistical office said that the production of aluminium and aluminium alloy wires had risen significantly in the same period.  We intend to pay close attention to further cable production developments in Central Europe before attributing a conclusive cause to the decline seen in early 2012 in Poland.  Our current forecast for Polish refined copper consumption is 255,000t in 2012, representing a decline of 3.0% y-o-y.

The rates of growth in China’s GDP and IP slowed in 2011 and are expected to decline further in 2012, which should impact the wire and cable industry gradually. In addition, building wire demand was subdued, as it was affected by the severe macro controls applied to the property market. One large sized wire and cable producer reported that its capacity utilization is about 60% at the moment, compared to running at full capacity last year. The difficulty it faces currently is that it is short of new orders, which are only one third the level of the same period last year. The air conditioner producers say that a high level of final product inventory continues to be a challenge. It is reported that air conditioner industry inventories are 1-1.5 times the normal level. We understand that domestic home appliance demand is also very weak currently, CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly April 2012 Chapter 1 28 attributed to the stimulus policy withdrawal, which brought forward demand during 2009 to 2011. Moreover, the recent Chinese residential construction floor space sold continues to decline, which is further constraining home appliance demand. This is a situation that is not expected to change in the short term, as the severe macro control of the property market will continue. We were told by one of the top three Chinese air conditioner producers that the weak demand is leading to a build up in inventories of their products. However, we heard reports that China’s Commercial Ministry may introduce an energy-saving appliances subsidy policy in the near future, which should boost domestic demand, but we do not have a specific schedule yet. Furthermore, refined copper demand in autos and electronics remains weak as well. Some market insiders expect that after the first year of adjustment in 2010, the auto sector might start picking up moderately as well in 2012.In terms of short term outlook, at the moment we tend to believe refined copper demand will struggle to recover in the usually robust seasonal way in April. China’s non-ferrous metals industry 12th five year plan, which will guide non-ferrous metals industry development, was anno

unced by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology in the beginning of 2012. According to the plan, China’s nonferrous metals demand is expected to continue to increase but the growth rate will slow down. Refined copper consumption was 7.53Mt in 2010 with average growth of 15% from 2005 to 2010 and is forecast to be 9.7Mt in 2015 with an average growth rate of 5.2% from 2011 to 2015. We are inclined to believe that the consumption goal in 2015 is conservative given the current consumption base. Nonetheless, we believe that the general development trend for the copper industry set out in the 12th five year plan is more important than the specific figures. At the same time non ferrous metals industry development plan accords with China’s economy develop plan from 2011 to 2015. In China’s 12th five year development plan, the average GDP growth target is 7% which is lower than the 7.5% average GDP growth rate in the past five years. 

The National People’s Congress and Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference ended in mid-March. China’s Premier Wen Jiabao announced that the GDP target was cut to 7.5% this year, which indicates that the government will not push GDP growth as strongly as before. The economy should therefore return to reasonable and sustainable growth. Some market insiders understand that GDP growth target at 7.5%, instead of the usual 8%, has sent a strong message that Chinese government does not mind a slower growth pace during the period of economic transformation, provided that social stability is not threatened. In addition, he announced that the regulation on real estate will not relax and house prices are a long way away from reaching a reasonable level, meaning that the severe macro control on the property market will continue. This will constrain copper consumption growth in property and related industries (e.g. household appliances). We estimated that refined copper consumption in building construction and home appliance and accessories accounted for about 34% of total refined copper usage in 2011.However, in positive news, there is increased scope for monetary policy to ease as inflation has declined, inflation is now back to more comfortable levels having dropped to an average of 3.9% in January and February, which will support demand in the future. Market insiders expect monetary easing to take place in H2 2012.

However, as indicated above we see it narrowing in 2016 due to the anticipated start up of some major new projects and the planned closure of smelting capacity in Australia. Ore grades** Our estimate of ore grades is based on quarterly ore grade data from a sample of 59 mines that accounted for one-third of total global copper production in Q4 2011. The sample average ore grade increased to 1.17% Cu in Q4 2011, up from 1.10% in Q3 and was the highest sample average ore grade registered since Q3 2008. Labour unrest** After a relatively turbulent Q4 2011 with strikes at the Grasberg and Cerro Verde mines and several labour disruptions to operations in Zambia, disruptions from labour unrest have been less frequent in Q1 2012. Most problems in Q1 stem from the previous quarter, including continuing unrest in Zambia and additional labour disputes at Grasberg. Overall, we believe that the risk of disruptions from labour unrest in the imminent future has diminished as fewer major labour contracts are up for negotiation this year. Following the 3-month labour dispute at the Grasberg mine, costing an estimated 115,000t of copper-in-concentrate production, the mine suffered from further, smaller labour-related disruptions in Q1 2012. On 23rd February, operations at Grasberg were once again suspended amid security concerns and unresolved issues between the management and the workers. The company claimed that the disruption was due to several acts of intimidation and violence against workers who did not participate in last year’s strike. However, the workers’ union alleged that workers had walked off the job in protest at the management’s failure to fulfil the agreement that ended last year’s strike. Workers returned to work on 12th March.

###### **3.2.3. Government issues** Continuing

the trend in recent years, Q1 2012 also witnessed several further instances of government behaviour that can be attributed to growing ‘resource nationalism’.  Recent measures imposed by governments are predominantly driven by tax revenue incentives in the light of soaring metals commodities prices and company profits.  They also serve as means of boosting popularity amongst nationalistic and environmentalist factions of the public, especially pre-election.  The key developments in Q1 include more restrictive investment regulations in Indonesia and the announcement of plans to increase tax rates in the DRC. 

In March, the Indonesian government announced a new regulation whereby the state or local companies will be eligible to acquire, at market value, at least a 51% stake in future foreignowned mining operations by the tenth year after commissioning.  It is believed that currently operating mines will not be affected until their mining licences are due for renewal. 

This development comes after the Indonesian government initiated in February talks with major foreign companies to renegotiate mining contracts.  Freeport-McMoRan is currently in talks with the government to renegotiate its contract for the Grasberg mine and Newmont mining has also agreed to review its mining contract for the Batu Hijau mine. 

Both of these developments are part of a previously announced government plan which aims to increase the government’s share in mining operations in the country.  Market insiders are

More recently, in March, the minister of mines in the DRC announced that the government is in the process of reviewing the existing mining code, which is 10 years old, in order to secure a higher share of the revenues from mining operations in the country.  According to the announcement, the new measures would include higher tax rates and greater ownership shares for the government.  In addition, the new mining code would also introduce regulation aimed at preventing unprocessed raw material from being exported and increasing the level of domestic processing and manufacturing.  Indonesia implemented similar legislation in February, banning the export of unprocessed minerals by the end of 2014. 

###### **3.2.4. Environmental issues** 

Environmental regulations and a tough government stance on environmental issues has been the norm in developed countries for many years.  However, environmental issues have recently gained growing importance in developing countries. 

In particular, in March, the Zambia Environmental Management Authority (ZEMA) ordered Glencore’s Mopani Copper Mines to shut down its M

ufulira heap leaching plant due to pollution violations.  ZEMA’s spokeswoman said that an inspection of the operation revealed that there was no acid mist or vapour barrier to prevent emissions. The agency suspects that the emissions of acid mist have caused an increase in pulmonary, throat, nose and ear ailments in the surrounding area. The operation would only be allowed to resume after implementation of rigorous environmental standards, according to a statement. 

Mopani copper mines subsequently announced that it will spend US$145M on an anti-pollution programme in the Copper Belt over the next two years. The project will mainly be focused on reducing the emissions of sulphur dioxide into the environment but will also include a project aimed at securing clean water supplies local residents. 

Shutdowns for environmental reasons are unusual in Zambia, and this may signal the beginning of more stringent environmental standards being applied in the country.  Indeed, the Ichimpe project in Northern Zambia is also under review by ZEMA as will be discussed in the projects section.  While this may raise costs for miners, improved environmental protection can only be positive for relations with the local communities and local employees.  Indeed, environmental damage is the most frequently cited reason for opposition to mining operations from local communities.

There have been few reports of infrastructure-related problems in Q1 2010.  The power infrastructures of Chile and Zambia have been largely unhindered during this period, with the Zambian government announcing vast investment plans into its power network.  In Chile and Australia, extreme weather events have disrupted some transport links, leading to minor production disruptions. 

The Energy Regulation Board (ERB) of Zambia has announced plans to increase current power generation capacity from 1,900MW to 3,500MW by 2015, with some developments already

###### **3.2.7. Natural hazards** 

Unexpectedly, Chile was the region most affected by natural hazards in Q1 2012, with several unseasonably severe weather events sweeping through the north of the country.  Meanwhile, the northern hemisphere endured its winter season, although no serious disruptions to mining were reported. 

The first reports of unseasonably severe weather conditions in northern Chile emerged in early January 2012, when the region was struck by heavy rain, snow and electrical storms, although no serious disruptions were reported.  The region houses some of the world’s largest mines, as well as major ports.  A month later, heavy rains in the region of Calama, in Chile’s Atacama desert, halted production at a number of mines, mainly for safety reasons.

The majority of these mines returned to normal operations within two days however, as the hazardous weather retreated.  Nonetheless, the Chuquicamata mine was directly affected by the heavy rains, causing production to be halted while operations at Radomiro Tomic were suspended as a precaution.  It is also likely that the El Abra mine was somewhat disrupted by the adverse weather conditions.  At Gaby and Ministro Hales some precautionary measures were put into place, but operations were not directly affected.

Nearby mines Spence, El Tesoro and Esperanza did not report any disruptions to production. 

The disruption was somewhat unexpected as the Atacama desert is regarded as the world’s driest region.  However, last year, production at some higher altitude mines north of Calama was also disrupted by unusual snowfall and heavy rains, indicating changing local weather patterns.  This can be particularly hazardous, as the area is ill-equipped for dealing with unexpected weather events, posing an increased risk of mine disruptions in the future. 

Again in mid-March, mining operations in Region I of northern Chile suffered from severe rainfall.  Local reports indicated that the resultant flash floods obstructed transport routes and overflowed into some operations.  Most notably, the Haldeman Mining Company, owners of the Sagasca mine, declared f _orce majeure_ on 13<sup>th</sup> March, following mudslides disrupting operations.  Furthermore, access roads to the Collahuasi and Cerro Colorado mines became impassable due to flooding and there have been unconfirmed reports of direct flooding on the grounds of the Collahuasi mine itself. 

Nonetheless, despite these disruptions, output was not greatly affected, with most production loss attributed to ore grade declines. We expect that weather related disruptions will pick up in Q2 as the southern hemisphere moves into the Autumn season. We recall miners facing similar unusual weather disruptions last year, with intermittent heavy rainfalls witnessed until mid2011.  Moreover, June marks the start of the rainy season in East Asia, that it usually associated with severe floods, especially in China. 

Besides rainfall, Chile also faced other natural hazards in Q1.  The central part of the country was hit by a 7.1 magnitude earthquake on 25<sup>th</sup> March.  However, no casualties were reported and there was no serious damage to infrastructure.  There are several major copper mines near the epicentre of the earthquake, including Codelco’s Andina and El Teniente and Anglo American’s Los Bronces.  However, operations at the mines were reported to be normal.  This is the largest earthquake to hit Chile, since the 8.8 magnitude tremor in 2010 that caused 500 fatalities and major destruction.

Hillgrove Resources Managing Director said that the setback is not expected to affect 2012 production, as the lost ground will be recovered in the course of the year. Greenfield projects are especially prone to delays or even failure as they usually require greater investment, a longer development period, are subject to a plethora of regulatory barriers and attract greater attention from local communities and pressure groups alike. In particular, on 14th January, it was announced that the Tampakan project in the Philippines was denied environmental clearance by the Philippine Department of Environmental and CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly April 2012 Chapter 2 49 Natural Resources (DENR). The project is owned by Sagittarius Mines Inc. (SMI), a joint venture between Xstrata and Indophil Resources NL. In other news, Ivanhoe Mines, majority owned by Rio Tinto, is facing problems in securing power supply for its Oyu Tolgoi project in Mongolia that is due to come on stream in six months.  The remote location of the deposit in the Gobi desert and generally poor infrastructure in Mongolia has made the development of the mine very challenging.  Securing a power source for the mining operations has presented some problems. 

The Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy of Mongolia estimates the total expected electricity demand from the Oyu Tolgoi project will be 200-310MW in the future.  With Mongolia’s aging power plant infrastructure already insufficient, this demand cannot be met by domestic sources. 

In 2008, Mongolia had an electricity generation capacity of around 3.2Gwh and consumption of 3.4Gwh.  The resulting energy deficit was offset by energy imports from Russia. Since then there has been a dramatic increase in power demand of around 6% annually since 2007. Moreover, with increasing mining activity in the country the pace of demand growth is expected to increase to 14% per annum in the future, according to the Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy of Mongolia.  Indeed, located in the same region as the Oyu Tolgoi project, South Gobi, is the biggest undeveloped coal deposit in the world, Tavan Tolgoi, which is also expected to become a major consumer of electricity in the future.  The Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy forecasts that total electricity demand from major South Gobi mines, including Oyu Tolgoi, will be around 870-1130MW. 

The original plan was for the Oyu Tolgoi mine to be connected to the Chinese power grid, across the border, in the first four years of operation.  The Oyu Tolgoi development plan includes the construction of a coal-fired power plant on site after four years, as the mining contract stipulates that all power must be sourced within Mongolia after this deadline. However, an agreement between China and Mongolia on the initial power grid connection deal has yet to be reached.  This could potentially cause serious delays to the existing production schedule.

###### **4.2.2 Raw material availability** 

###### **Concentrates** 

Copper-in-concentrate mine production in Q1 2012 continued to face disruptions, however it proved somewhat more settled than in the preceding quarter.  In fact, many of the problems witnessed in Q1 were linked to disruptions that emerged in Q4 2011.  Labour unrest continued to disrupt production, with the continuation of strikes in Zambia and intermittent episodes of unrest at Grasberg.  Low ore grades continued to affect production at many major mines, and although Q4 2011 witnessed an uptick in ore grades in our sample of 48 concentrates mines, we believe that this was attributed to miners targeting richer ore bodies ahead of their end-of-year production targets.  We therefore anticipate that ore grades are likely to have declined in Q1 2012 as miners return to normal production.  Other

disruptions included severe weather conditions in northern Chile and northern Australia, however, the impact of these was marginal, and no major infrastructure or technical problems were reported in Q1. Looking at copper concentrate grades, the grades of Chilean exported material declined in 2011 on average by about 0.9%. This follows a steady 2010 which saw grades staying flat and almost unchanged from the 30.66% average of 2009. The decline in 2011 is mainly attributed to Escondida, whose exports account for about 27% of the total Chilean concentrates exports. Escondida’s concentrates grades declined by 3.5% to 30.0%. If Escondida’s concentrate grades CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly April 2012 Chapter 2 59 had remained flat, the Chilean average concentrate grade for exported material would have in fact increased slightly to 30.7%, as most other miners showed minor rises (i.e. 0.1% to 0.3%) Looking ahead, we expect 2012 copper-in-concentrate production (after all disruptions) to reach 12.5Mt, representing y-o-y growth of just 0.7%. We expect decreased production in Indonesia on account of the Grasberg mine continuing to face labour disruptions and the Batu Hijau mine needing to process low grade stockpiled ore. In South and Central America, meanwhile, we have downgraded our production estimates at the Collahuasi and the Los Pelambres mines. In the long term, we believe that the growth in copper-in-concentrate production will gather pace from 2013, when a plethora of projects are expected to come on stream. After applying all probabilities and adjustments, these mine projects will add approximately 4.6Mt/y of copper-in-concentrate to mine production capacity by 2016. However, the recent surge in resource nationalistmeasures, especially in up-and-coming mining regions such a Zambia or the DR Congo, may trigger investor trepidation and lead to potential project delays or even cancellations in the future. ###### **4.2.3 Other disruptions** 

###### **Technical issues** 

Further to the shutdown of PASAR’s Leyte smelter in the Philippines following a January fire, it was announced on 20<sup>th</sup> March that the smelter is expected to resume operations in June or July. The fire had damaged the sulphuric acid plant at the smelter and new equipment has been ordered from China. The smelter is technically operational but cannot operate without sulphur capture due to the Philippines’ environmental regulations. No estimates were given of the expected production losses from the six-month shutdown. The Leyte smelter has an annual capacity of 210,000t copper-in-blister.  While the six-month shutdown of the smelter is a major disruption, the impact of the outage on the market has been relatively muted and, to our knowledge, the company has not declared _force majeure_ . This was possible due to Glencore’s (78% owner of PASAR) role as a major trader in both the concentrates and refined copper markets, enabling the company to divert the incoming raw materials meant for the smelter to the spot market via its trading arm and also secure supplies of refined copper to cover its supply commitments. 

Another shutdown took place at Pan Pacific Copper’s (PPC) 470,000t/y Saganoseki smelter in the southern province of Oita in Japan, where a high voltage cabling plant and an electric power substation were damaged due to fire. The smelter was closed for around six weeks, beginning 7<sup>th</sup> January, and resumed operations in 13<sup>th</sup> February.  An estimated 30,000t of cathode production were lost as a result of the closure, however, deliveries are said to have remained unaffected due to high stocks of anode.  PPC intends to make up this loss in production by postponing the maintenance of the Tamano smelter to autumn. The Tamano smelter was also reported to have been experiencing production problems.  A malfunctioning boiler caused the smelter to shut down from 6<sup>th</sup> to 21<sup>st</sup> February. 

Lastly, China’s Zijin Mining Group’s smelting project in Longyan City, Fujian Province, was forced to suspend operations on 25<sup>th</sup> January for an investigation after three workers died in an industrial accident at their sulphuric acid plant. The smelter was in the early days of a trial production period that was due to end on 15<sup>th</sup> June 2012. The plant has a full production capacity of 200,000t/y.

###### **Cutbacks and closures** 

The 320,000t/y Gresik smelter in Indonesia is due for major maintenance in May. The previous one took place in 2008 and the company says that regular plans for such maintenance are due every four years. 

Mitsubishi Materials Corp. plans to close its 270,000t/y Onahama smelting plant for a planned twenty-

day maintenance period beginning in mid-October 2012. This follows the reopening of the plant on 1<sup>st</sup> July 2011, after it had been damaged during the 11<sup>th</sup> March earthquake. From July, the facility was operating at 65% capacity, before returning to full capacity on 3<sup>rd</sup> September. On 5<sup>th</sup> October, _force majeure_ was lifted on shipments of copper concentrate to the plant. 

The maintenance of PPC’s 260,000t/y Tamano smelter in Japan has been postponed from AprilMay to the autumn of this year, in order to offset the production loss experienced at the Saganoseki smelter during its five-week shutdown caused by a fire in January. 

For 2013, we are aware that there are plans for major maintenance at Atlantic Copper’s 300,000t/y Huelva smelter in Spain. 

###### **Environmental/Government issues** 

The government of Peru announced that it will support plans to restart Doe Run Peru’s 75,000t/y La Oroya smelter. The restart is expected on 1<sup>st</sup> May 2012, subject to Peru’s congress approving a bill for the extension of a clean-up programme at the plant.  The strongest argument for reopening the smelter is the creation of around 3,500 jobs and indirect benefits to the local mining sector. The smelter has already received a 30-month extension to the clean-up in September 2009, which expired in March 2012. The clean-up, which entails cutting back sulphur dioxide emissions, is over half-way complete, however, it requires a further US$168M of investment to finalise. The plant has remained shut since June 2009 as a result of financial difficulties caused by the economic crisis.  Upon reopening, the plant’s operators hope to embark on a US$200M expansion plan, which will be financed by Glencore (US$135M) and the Renco Group (US$65M).  Glencore is said to supply most of the concentrates, with the rest coming from small and medium-sized local mines. Renco, Doe Run Peru’s parent company, is currently suing the Peruvian government, one of its creditors, for US$800M over allegedly breaching equal-treatment clauses in the US-Peru free trade agreement.  It has been suggested that the government hopes for these charges to be dropped in return for its support for the smelter’s reopening. CRU believes that the destiny of La Oroya remains uncertain and it appears unlikely that it will resume operations in the short run due to the political tension surrounding the current situation.  However, we believe that it is probable that the smelter will reopen in the long term. 

###### **Industrial action** 

In early February, operations were halted at Anglo American’s Chagres smelter in Chile after subcontractors staged a labour strike. The union of workers of subcontractor Tranex (involved in the logistics of concentrates and ores) blocked access to the smelter, claiming that Anglo American was restricting the right of the workers to unionize. The Confederacion of Trabajadores del Cobre (CTC), a major Chilean organization of wor

kers in copper, supported the strike.

###### **4.2.4 The sulphuric acid market** 

Sulphuric acid market participants became more cautious following the fires at the Asian smelters in January.  At the time, the acid market was quiet amidst an uncertain economic outlook, negotiations for annual contracts were progressing at varying speeds in different regions and acid prices were declining across all regions. In Peru and Chile, contracts had finalised at US$145-165/t CFR; in Europe, negotiations for Q1 were delayed as the market was in balance and the Japanese market was still affected by the closure of some copper smelters for maintenance. In China, the market was weakening ahead of the Lunar New Year with prices falling. 

The Saganoseki smelter restarted on 13<sup>th</sup> February, whereas the PASAR smelter is expected to be closed until June or July, which would imply some 240,000t of total losses of sulphuric acid. In addition, on 26<sup>th</sup> January, activities were suspended at Zijin Copper Industry following an accident at their sulphuric acid plant, which has a capacity of 850,000t/y. 

In a follow-up to the fires, the world balance remained in surplus as Chinese customers were absent from the market while celebrating the Lunar New Year. Before the holiday, the price in China was in the range of RMB200-450/t (US$32-63/t) for smelter=based acid and RMB350500/t for sulphur-burnt acid. Negotiations that were ongoing were due to resume by early February. Acid from South Korea and Japan that would normally be shipped to China was directed to other customers, putting some downward pressure on prices in other regions – mainly the Americas. 

Prices for Q1 contracts in Europe declined by €5-10/t CFR from Q4 settlements. So far, volumes requested in 2012 remain similar to the ones in 2011, but the uncertainty is reflected in the prices. The main change has been some buyers shifting from longer-term contracts to quarterly or half-yearly ones. In late January, the market was long. Suppliers were willing to deliver more acid if required but there was little demand for extra tonnage. In the Mediterranean, prices had been falling even further on the back of weak fundamentals, hitting €50/t in late January. 

The North American market has been long as a result of acid becoming more available in Asia and Europe, with prices below US$120/t CFR in January and approaching US$100/t during the Chinese holiday. Also, the Q1 2012 US Tampa sulphur price saw a $48/mt reduction to $172/mt FOB Tampa. This prompts the question of whether domestic producers will need to import acid with the sulphur price so low. The South American market is also well covered via contracted cargoes. The surplus of acid in the global market also put pressure on Chilean prices, which declined to US$115-125/t CFR. The Noracid plant re-started briefly but production problems forced it to close

again. The major smelters were still holding out for terms of $30/3.0¢ or more, and apparently some deals were made at these levels in mid-January for material into China. However, the closure of two smelters in -January - PASAR’s Leyte and PPC’s Saganoseki - due to damage stet by fires freed material to be released into the market

and boosted terms into the $40/4.0¢s. Numbers in the $50/5.0¢s were beginning to be heard in February for material going into China, due to subdued buying activity. However, the Saganoseki smelter was able to restart on 13th February and another strike-related production shutdown at Grasberg at the end of February saw spot terms between miners and traders sink to the high $20/2.0¢s. _Force majeure_ was not declared by PASAR, despite the most recent reports indicating that the plant will be out until at least July this year. Market sources indicate that majority owner Glencore has been able to divert incoming concentrate shipments to other smelters in Asia - and to meet its refined supply commitments via its trading stocks. The Indian smelters are said to be short of material at present, in part due to some shipping delays caused by a bankruptcy to Allied Shipping and another ship laden with supplies running aground. ###### **Contract Terms** 

The negotiations over the annual frame contract terms for 2012 are almost at a close, and this time around we have seen further unravelling of the traditional benchmark system.  Following Freeport McMoRan’s agreements at terms of $63.5/6.35¢ with all of its smelter customers, the other large miners went on to make different agreements elsewhere – with Codelco and BHPB agreeing terms of $60/6¢ in China and India and Anglo American agreeing $60.5/6.05¢ in Asia and at one Japanese smelter.  More recently, it has been rumoured that Anglo has agreed $62.5/6.25¢ with the other Japanese smelters - with the exception of PPC - and the European smelters.  We are informed that PPC are refusing to countenance terms lower than $63.5/6.35¢, and given that Anglo has made numerous agreements elsewhere that have been at lower terms than this, a holiday might end up being taken between these two companies for 2012.  This follows earlier reports that BHPB and Teck have taken a holiday from this year’s frame contracts with the Japanese smelters, after failing to reach agreements on TC/RCs. 

Antofagasta and Teck again sought to achieve lower TC/RCs than the other frame contracts for their high grade concentrates from the Los Pelambres and Highland Valley mines, respectively. We hear that they were both able to make agreements with Chinese smelters at terms of around $58/5.8¢ for their high grade mines, and that Antofagasta secured a $3.0/0.3¢ discount to the “Japanese benchmark” of $63.5/6.35¢ with its Japanese customers. 

Elsewhere, we understand that many of the smaller and medium sized miners accepted Freeport’s numbers as the benchmark, and we learned that Codelco eventually agreed $63.5/6.35¢ with the Japanese smelters, though with a 50% tonnage cut for PPC.  Also, miners with high gold content in their concentrates tend to prefer to sell to the Japanese smelters and so Newmont, Newcrest and Ok Tedi Mining all opted to agree 2012 terms at the Japanese benchmark. (In the case of Newcrest, there were apparently some concessions on the side terms, including a reduction in average minimum copper concentrate grades according to some reports.)

Equally, it has been suggested that the drawdown was constituted by improving sentiment about US economic prospects and in turn copper consumption.  However, this is not yet evident in US spot cathode purchases.  Spot deals remained few and far between in March.  It is too early to say with conviction that there has actually been an increase in consumption and, if so, whether or not this is being met through annual contract material instead of spot metal.  As a result of the low level of spot activity, premia have remained roughly the same throughout Q1 at 5.756.25¢/lb, supported by high gasoline prices that are boosting the freight element. 

With neither consumption nor exports sufficient reasons for the sudden decline in stock in New Orleans, and subsequently St Louis, we believe that there are two possible other explanations. Someone may have taken the metal out of the LME system to help foster an impression of physical tightness.  A flat forward curve, to hedge the price downside, and cheap financing mean a large financial player could be betting on the deficit forecast for 2012 coming true.  If it does, prices and premia should rise and they would profit handsomely.  As New Orleans open tonnage bottomed out, the decline in open tonnage in St Louis mirrored that of New Orleans, but this could be attributed to a ‘jumping on the band wagon’ effect.  Traders who have come to rely on LME warehouses for copper over the past few years may have panicked a bit as they saw the New Orleans metal disappear.  Once they saw that St Louis warrants were being cancelled, they may have jumped in to secure tonnages for their use later in the Spring to meet seasonally stronger demand.  There have also been draw downs of cathode out of Chicago LME warehouses and COMEX warehouses, but this is less marked than in either New Orleans or St Louis and the decline at those locations seems more reflective of actual consumption. 

###### European copper demand steadies 

The outlook on European copper consumption has improved in the last quarter.  The misnamed Long Term Refinancing Operation (LTRO) three-year loan programme by the European Central Bank means that the sovereign debt crisis will not immediately translate into a banking crisis. Nonetheless, we still expect consumption to decline this year, as the Eurozone goes into recession, however, a catastrophic collapse seems to have been averted.  Spot demand for cathode was supported by the delay to some imported material earlier in the month.  Low levels of both LME stocks in the region and annual contract volumes have meant that this quickly translated into higher premia.  Those on material for deliver

y to a Northwest European port jumped to over $100/t, but in late March fell back to $80-100/t. With concerns over rising Spanish bond yields showing the crisis is not solved, European debt problems will continue to weigh on the copper market. ###### Production remains disrupted We estimate that total copper mine production in Q1 2012 reached 4.24Mt, up just 0.1% from the previous quarter. Copper-in-concentrate production rose by 0.7% q-o-q, reaching 3.21Mt in Q1, whereas, EW cathode production declined by 3.2% q-o-q to 0.90Mt. In spite of the slight overall uptick in output, Q1 remained a largely disrupted period as far as mine production was concerned. The most prominent disruption during this period came from continuing labour unrest in many mining regions. Most notably, the Grasberg mine in Indonesia experienced a resurgence of labour disputes, despite the end of a three-month strike in mid-December. The surge of strikes that swept through Zambia in Q4 2011 continued to disrupt production at a number of mines in Q1 of this year. Nonetheless, labour disruptions settled down in most of South and Central America, especially in Chile and Peru. Another factor that underlined much CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly April 2012 Chapter 3 81 of the production loss in Q1 was the continuing ore grade decline, which was felt especially strongly by many of the world’s largest mines. Natural hazards also caused some mine production problems in the first quarter, especially the unexpectedly severe rains in northern Chile. Short term market outlook ###### Growth expected to draw high Shanghai stocks down We believe that the current phase of rising imports in China will begin to unwind in Q2. The consumption outlook for H1 in China is not as buoyant as previously expected. The build up in stocks to levels above last year will give pause to those using copper as part of a wider trading strategy, as the

scope for the market to absorb ever higher stock levels is less than previously expected.  We therefore anticipate that imports will decline sharply from April. 

As for Chinese copper consumption, it did strengthen seasonally after the New Year, just not as much as market participants had hoped.  In part this is due to a build up in end-use products (such as domestic appliances) that need to be worked down before demand for copper semis can accelerate rapidly.  With monetary loosening expected to come through in H2, we forecast that consumption growth will begin to speed up in China later this year.  Due to this slower start, we now forecast that copper consumption growth for the year as a whole will accelerate only slightly in 2012, to 6.3% from the 5.9% growth we estimate for 2011. 

We expect domestic Chinese refined production (including an allowance for adjustments) to rise this year from 1.34Mt in Q1 to 1.45Mt by Q4.  This is slightly below the pace of growth in 2011, helping to rebalance the physical cathode market. 

As a result of the severe oversupply in the country, we expect Chinese exports to rise to over 20,000t/m and imports to fall below 200,000t/m (the monthly average required to feed demand not met by domestic production) in Q2.  In part, the increase in exports will come from some of the Chinese smelters that have a license to export cathode on a tolling basis.  This scheme allows them to export cathode equivalent to 20-30% of their prior year imports of concentrates to help maintain higher utilisation rates. 

As the domestic physical market for cathode tightens due to it moving into deficit, the premium for imported cathode should then bottom out.  Therefore, the high stocks built up on SHFE and in bonded warehouses can begin to be run down.  We anticipate that the latter will fall by 325,000t over the course of Q2-Q4, before beginning to rebound in Q4 in the usual seasonal pattern ahead of seasonally stronger demand in Q1 of next year. 

This mixed picture for the fundamentals, along with an equally mixed outlook for the influence of investors, means we forecast that the price will only rise modestly on throughout 2012 to an average of $8,660/t in Q4.  These averages, though, conceal a much more volatile trading range that we expect could be $7,750/t and $9,250. 

###### Parallel supply and consumption growth to leave market in deficit in 2013 

We expect 42 mining projects to come on stream in 2012.  However, the full effect on production will be delayed until 2013, as the new operations are expected to ramp up gradually. With additional projects coming on stream in 2013, aggregate mine production is expected to increase by 1.25Mt. Growth in refined production is therefore forecast to mirror that of the mines, up by 7.2% in 2013.

Medium term outlook ###### Supply surge to bring prices down An even larger wave of production from new projects is expected to begin to come on in 2014 and continue through the end of the forecast period, with mine output forecast to rise by 5.3% in 2014. A reshuffling of mine projects mean that growth in refined output will be slightly less robust than previously expected in 2014 but still over 1Mt that year and the next. A bunching of mine projects in 2016 is expected to produce a 1.3Mt spurt in refined output that year. This unprecedented growth is expected to swell mine output by 4.3Mt on the level of 15.9Mt we estimate for 2011, which equates to a 27% rise over the outlook period. Following the over 5% rise in consumption in 2013 due to the synchronised, cyclical macroeconomic upswing, we forecast that consumption growth will average over 4% in 2014-16. The combination of some production pushed further out with a higher profile for consumption means we now see the market moving into balance in 2014. This should be accompanied by the price falling in the second half of the year, which will drag the annual average down towards $8,000/t. A move into surplus as higher mine production feeds through will lead to only a modest build in stocks in 2015, which should support the price at around $8,000/t. By 2016, though, a surplus of 560,000t will boost stock levels and push up the reported stock to consumption ratio to 2.7 weeks. As more projects are forecast to come on just beyond the current forecast horizon, the influence of financial players in the market will begin to turn negative and the price is forecast to fall to an average of just under $7,500/t ($3.40/lb) in the final year of the period. This decline in the price will dent margins for miners, but as the chart below shows, the average mine, as calculated in CRU’s mine cost model, will see a gross margin of over 100% through to 2015. This is both a blessing and a curse, as we have seen over the pa

st few years. It is a blessing because profits are high and allow companies to explore for new supply. It is a curse because workers and governments in countries hosting miners will continue to eye these large gross profits and look to raise their share of the revenue pie, which will make it ever more challenging for miners to successfully bring on the new capacity required to meet projected demand. ###### Key risks to the price outlook In 2012, risks to the price around the base case are fairly balanced, as the range forecast in the chart above demonstrates. Downside macroeconomic and financial risks and their consequent negative impact on consumption are offsetting the upside risks of lower copper production and higher investor inflows into copper. One point to note is that Chinese buying when the price falls below $7,000/t, in unison with a contraction in Chinese mine output, provide a floor for the price. In 2013, the risks move to about 3:1 to the upside, with production risks dominating. From 2014 to 2016, the risks become slightly less biased, but remain to the upside driven principally by production possibly underperforming compared to the base case. ###### Production risks Production risks to the price are mostly to the upside. The first is that insufficient availability of equipment, qualified personnel, water, power, etc. mean that sequencing of projects (at both the company and industry levels) will be a serious challenge. We believe that there is a greater downside than upside risk to our production forecast and therefore an upward bias to the price forecast. There is some downside risk from production. We have a disruption allowance in the 20142016 period of 13% and have made allowances for project risks of 10% for firm, 30% for probable and 60% for possible. If our macroeconomic forecast turns out as too optimistic, then demand could be less and the wave of mine projects could come on just in time to swamp the market and drive down prices sooner than in our base case. ###### Macroeconomic and financial risks The key risk to the copper price is the uncertainty of how the global economy will perform. The apparent improvement in the US could prove short lived and China could possibly not see a return to growth in H2 2012. The Eurozone crisis could also still prompt more financial market turmoil. CRU International Limited confidential 90 Copper Quarterly April 2012 Chapter 3 On the other hand, economic growth in both the US and China could prove stronger than

forecast in the base case.  This would be positive for growth in these important consuming countries, but also in those emerging markets which export to these two large economies. 

###### Consumption risks 

###### Downside 

Aluminium producers are currently facing challenging conditions, with the industry in a situation of chronic oversupply.  Smelter closures have finally begun, with many of the closures directly impacting captive hot metal wirerod plants at aluminium smelters.  So, despite a Cu:Al price ratio of around 3.8:1, supply constraints are likely to prevent aluminium from increasing its market share in the rod sector in the short term.  Longer term though, the substitution threat remains significant for copper demand growth in wirerod.  We expect aluminium will make more inroads into the insulated power cable market as a result of an increase in aluminium wirerod capacity available to target this segment by 2015. 

CRU forecasts that the ratio of the copper price to that of aluminium will average close to 4:1, which will weigh on all consumers’ strategic decision-making. 

Although the emerging markets are performing well, driven by domestic demand, there are ongoing concerns about inflationary pressures.  Copper consumption would be negatively affected by emerging market governments introducing anti-inflationary policies which would dent economic growth. 

###### Upside 

The potential shortage of scrap for direct use (due to weaker generation) could lead to additional cathode requirements, especially in China. 

A double-dip recession would only accelerate the emerging markets decoupling their economic growth further from the industrialised countries by favouring copper-intensive domestic demand. 

Some Chinese consumers or the SRB could see copper as a bargain for speculative purposes at prices much lower than our base case, thus leading to higher cathode imports.  As a result of RMB appreciation, further support for copper could also emerge from a diversion of surplus cash away from the dollar and directly into commodity investments as a means of diversification.

###### 5. Investor activity 

###### 5.1 LME price movements 

During January and February, LME metals were on a generally rising trend, but prices fell during March. Beginning in mid-January and through mid-February, LME metals prices rose as the euro appreciated against the US dollar, thanks to a second bailout for Greece that was finally agreed on 21 February 2012.  In addition, the economic data releases pointed to a lower likelihood of a drastic slowdown in the region. Although China’s manufacturing activity remained muted, it appeared more likely to hold steady than to decelerate further. With inflation relatively under control, Beijing’s policymakers retained the ability to implement policies to stimulate growth, rather than restrain it.  Finally, a potential EU oil embargo against Iran, civil unrest in Syria and a stronger euro/weaker US dollar pushed Brent crude oil prices higher, which attracted index fund investors and helped to push metals prices higher as well. 

Through the end of February, metals prices were relatively range bound as the markets waited to see exactly how Greece’s private sector debt would be restructured. The markets turned their attention to China, and noticed just how much copper was being stockpiled. This, along with the usual lack of available economic data for January and February, caused investors to hesitate about committing too much to the LME metals complex. Greece finally came to terms with its private creditors on 9 March 2012, with the majority of bondholders agreeing to take significant write downs. As of 5 April 2012, 97% of the bondholders had agreed to participate in the debt swap, paving the way for the release of additional funds from the IMF. However, concerns over Spain have surfaced again, so the euro has stopped gaining against the US dollar and this has kept LME metals prices from increasing any further.

###### 1. Oil shock threat looms larger 

Despite the tangible improvement in sentiment following the European Central Bank’s (ECB) longer term refinancing operation (LTRO) we’ve maintained our downbeat view with respect to the Eurozone because we believe that all the programme did was buy the financial sector and governments a little more time, rather than change the fundamentals. **In the absence of a fresh stimulus to growth the developed economies remain locked into an arduous recovery at best.** As if that wasn’t enough the **renewed threat of an oil shock** is throwing its shadow over the global outlook as a whole.

###### 2. Regional developments 

###### 2.1 The Americas: US recovery maintains momentum 

In the final analysis US GDP growth in the fourth quarter was revised up to 3% q/q annualised. **Subsequently growth’s eased, as the temporary factors at work at the end of 2011 have subsided.** Nonetheless, high frequency data, relating to employment, retail sales including autos, and manufacturing, reinforce our view that the **USA is recovering steadily, and on course to gain a little momentum beyond the first quarter** .  This is as we expect, but still at a pace well below that evident in past upturns. 

Non farm payrolls increased by a net 227,000 in February. **This was the third consecutive month in which employment rose by more than 200,000.** But due to an increase in the participation rate the unemployment rate stayed put at 8.3%, versus 9.1% six months ago. 

**Consumer confidence has improved as a result of the firming labour market, and this is translating into stronger consumer spending.** Thus retail sales expanded by 1.1% m/m in February.  This was their fastest rate of growth in five months, and it lifted them 6.5% y/y.   The pick up was led by autos which rose 6.4%, following a 4.7% m/m rise in January.  The steady

rise in retail sales has helped keep the inventory to sales ratio steady at 1.27 months for the past half year. 

The underlying advance in retail sales, allied with stock replenishment, and helped at the margin by exports, continues to support output.  Although industrial production stagnated in February **manufacturing output increased by 0.4% m/m** .  In fact it was held back by a contraction in auto assembly, which was to an extent a payback after the strong 8.6% m/m gain in January.   Recent survey data points to further output growth in the near term.  Encouragingly the volume of unfilled manufacturing orders rose 0.6% m/m in January. 

What this amounts to is evidence that the recovery is sustained, and gaining in traction. However, as we’ve argued before, **it’s very modest given the depth of the downturn in 2009, and compared with the pace of earlier upswings** . 

**This is evident first and foremost in the labour market.** In addition to its inflation mandate the Federal Reserve (Fed) is tasked with maintaining the economy at full employment, which equates to an unemployment rate around 5%.   However, we’re unlikely to see an acceleration sufficient to transform the labour market to this extent any time soon.  A recent survey showed that a majority of employers remain reluctant to hire in the short term.  Thus the labour market continues to mend slowly, and will struggle to up this performance as federal layoffs gather pace in 2013.  Put another way, **output growth would have to pick up to something like 4% per year for a sustained period to bring the unemployment rate towards the full employment target swiftly, implying net job creation in the 300,000400,000 per month range** .  As things stand full employment is unlikely to be reached until the turn of the decade. 

**The factors holding firms back from ramping up their recruitment appear to be similarly holding back investment.** This is why we have business investment expanding 2-3 percentage points more slowly in this recovery than for example in the upturn after the recession in the early 1990s.

**Businesses are exercising great caution in their hiring and capital spending partly because consumer spending continues to face headwinds.** Apart from anything else income growth is modest at best.  According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics median weekly income has fallen 2% since the official end of the recession in mid 2009, although recent data suggests that that trend was arrested in the second half of 2011.  What’s more personal savings data indicates that a rising share of any incremental income is being saved.  Partly that reflects uncertainties about the jobs market, although worries of that sort should be diminishing now. As, or more importantly, household balance sheets are still under pressure, because although equity prices have been buoyant house prices remain weak. 

On some mea

sures equity prices have recovered by 20% from the trough in late 2011.  In contrast house prices, measured by the Case-Schiller index, were down by 4% y/y in December, and 30% below the peak hit in 2006.  At the onset of the crisis housing accounted for about 40% of total investment. **With a significant pipeline of foreclosed homes still in place the hole in housing’s share of investment will take many quarters to repair,** despite evidence of improvements in housing market activity. 

**That said deleveraging in the USA has progressed further than in most other developed economies.** Aggregate debt has fallen from almost 300% of GDP in 2008 to 279% in mid 2011. Other heavily indebted economies started the crisis under far heavier debt piles, and have made much less progress.  This is a key reason why the USA is outperforming most other developed economies.  Unfortunately government debt in the USA is as problematic as elsewhere, and herein lies a particular risk: if the election in November produces a legislative stalemate which makes it impossible to reach a compromise on the expiry of the slew of temporary tax cuts at the end of 2012 a fiscal shock will ensue.  In our base case we assume most of these tax cuts are extended beyond 2012. 

In the meantime another risk is coming to the fore. **Rising oil prices could compromise the Fed’s ability to keep monetary policy ultra loose.** The rate of increase in headline consumer prices picked up in January, from 0.2% m/m the previous month to 0.4%, which was the fastest increase in the CPI in almost a year, and it was attributable in particular to a 6% m/m rise in gasoline costs.  Yields on treasury bonds have increased in recent days in response.  Very low interest rates out into 2014 cannot be taken for granted. 

**Brazil’s economy slowed to grow by only 2.7% y/y in 2011,** down from a heady 7.5% in 2010.  This was mainly due to the slowdown in the Eurozone, but the sharp appreciation of the real caused by considerable inflows of capital, attracted by high domestic interest rates, strengthened the currency and weakened the export sector. 

Official confirmation of the disappointing 2011 figures has added pressure on the central bank to continue its present easing cycle.  Investment, for example, grew only 4.7% y/y in 2011 after reaching over 21% in 2010.  Furthermore, industrial output fell to 1.6% y/y in 2011 from a 10.4% gain the previous year.  In response, **the central bank cut the Selic interest rate in March by 75 bp to 9.75%.** 

While 2011 was relatively disappointing, **recent high frequency data suggest that some areas of the economy are improving.** The manufacturing PMI, for example, signalled further improvement in the sector.  The indicator rose for the fifth consecutive month in February to
