g firms added to their workforces for the second consecutive month in February, with the rate of job creation the strongest since March 2011. 

**Our outlook hasn’t changed** : we have expected relatively lower growth for some time as part of our belief that the economy bottomed out in the second half of last year.  We forecast relatively weak growth of 3.1% this year, followed by a return to trend growth of between 4- 4.8% throughout the period 2013-2016. 

###### 2.2 Europe: Eurozone far from safe 

European authorities have made some progress in stemming the crisis that threatened to engulf the region towards the end of 2011. **In particular, the ECB’s recent interventions have significantly calmed financial markets, and helped avert a potentially catastrophic credit crunch.** Furthermore, Greece has managed to secure **a new round of bailout funding and has negotiated a debt swap** aimed at reducing its debt burden, albeit at the expense of even deeper spending cuts, and closer monitoring of its finances.  However, we **remain sceptical** that this will be enough to solve Greece’s fiscal mess in the long-run.  Also, the let up in bank funding pressures since December has **not translated into lending** to the real economy, which is showing signs of further deterioration as 2012 progresses.  Broadly positive developments since last month have also been countered by the effects of **rising oil prices** , which now threaten to constrain any recovery in the consumer sector, by reducing real incomes, and, in the corporate sector, by hitting businesses with higher input costs, which are already suffering from weak demand at home and abroad. 

**Eurozone financial markets have improved in recent weeks** , aided by a further injection of liquidity from the ECB in late February.  The 3-year lending operation – **LTRO** – saw around 800 banks borrowing €530 bn, resulting in a net liquidity injection of around €300 bn. In the space of two months, the ECB has now injected over €1 trn of money into the financial system, **banishing the threat of a credit crunch, which was a major worry in late 2011** .  The fact that 800 banks used the latest LTRO – compared with 492 in December – suggests that a greater number of smaller banks gained access to funding, helped by the ECB's decision to expand the range of eligible collateral.  Banks in the peripheral countries have been the heaviest users of the LTRO, being the ones that faced the hardest liquidity squeeze in interbank markets. Spanish and Italian banks are now financing around 5% of their assets from the ECB, and some of the **LTRO funds have been recycled into increased purchases of government debt, helping bring down yields from the dangerous levels seen late last year.** 

Financial markets have also been buoyed up by the agreement of a **€130 bn second bail-out package for Greece, and a debt swap process.** Greece has managed to slash its debts by more than €100 bn by swapping privately held bonds for

new, longer maturity paper with less than half the nominal value. The swap was accepted by 85% of bondholders and means that the **imminent risk of a disorderly default by Greece has receded.** However, despite the improvement in financial conditions, **the real economy has continued to struggle. Rising oil prices** mean that inflationary pressures are returning. The ECB now forecasts it to be higher, at between 2.1 and 2.7% this year, and well above the ECB's target of close to but below 2%. Not only does this put pressure on disposable incomes, hitting CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly April 2012 – Appendix A 105 consumption, but businesses face higher fuel costs, reducing profitability. Higher inflation also **means interest rates are unlikely to be reduced this year or next.** **Furthermore, the ECB’s LTRO programme has failed to increase lending to the real economy.** As of January, bank lending to non-financial corporations was still decelerating in the Eurozone as a whole, shrinking in peripheral countries and rising only slowly in core countries (particularly Germany). Credit availability is expected to remain tight, particularly as bank lending will be influenced by the need to raise capital ratios (to meet Basel III requirements) and the weak economic outlook. Meanwhile, **the industrial sector continues to struggle** . Underpinned by energy and investment goods, industrial output increased in January (by 0.2% m/m) for the first time since October. Nonetheless, the expansion was weaker than expected as foreign demand remains muted, while domestic demand is squeezed by higher inflation. **GDP shrank by 0.3% q/q in the final quarter of 2011, and we expect similar falls in the first half of this year.** Growth will continue to be suffocated by **major austerity programmes** as they ramp up across the region, combined with a **lack of growth-enhancing reforms** to counter-balance the effects. **As a result, unemployment, particularly in the public-sector, is set to rise this year to around 11%,** with a wide divergence between the core and periphery. The situation is particularly dire for Spain, where the jobless rate hit 23.3% in January.  Youth unemployment – measuring workers under the age of 25 – was just shy of 50%.  Meanwhile, the jobless rate was just 4% in Austria, 5% in the Netherlands and 5.8% in Germany. 

**Finally, business confidence in the Eurozone remains weak,** as the debt crisis lingers, and consumer demand remains anaemic.  Although the Economic Sentiment Indicator (ESI) rose for the second month in a row in February by 1 point to 94.4, it remains well below its long-term average of 100.  This will be a **drag on hiring and capital spending in coming months. Overall, we continue to forecast a recession for 2012 overall, with varying degrees of severity in the different member states. **The situation in Germany remains relatively buoyant.** The composite PMI, although falling to 53.2 in February from 53.9 in the previous month, was still higher than in any month of the fourth quarter, and the composite new orders index posted an expansion for the first time since July last year. Furthermore, the ZEW indicator, which also polls economic expectations for the next six months, but based on the views of analysts, turned positive in February for the first time since May last year. 

However, other data at the beginning of the year are consistent with the weak growth rates we expect.  Although consumer confidence is strong, buoyed up by record low unemployment, **German consumers remain reluctant to spend** , with retail sales down 1.6% m/m in January. Industrial production was up by 1.6% m/m in January, but only after a sharp fall of 2.6% in the previous month.  This in part may reflect the weakening outlook in the rest of the continent - some 60% of Germany’s exports go to the Eurozone. Even if it does implement these measures, growth is likely to take a significant hit, putting further strain on public finances and debt sustainability **. **In Central and Eastern Europe,** most economies saw positive growth in the final quarter of 2011, with Poland leading the way with 1.1% q/q growth (leaving growth at an impressive 4.4% for 2011 as a whole), albeit consumer spending increased at its slowest pace since 2009. The slowdown in China is largely a response to the domestic policy tightening that was implemented to rein in an over exuberant real estate sector and escalating inflation, although, clearly, the weakness of overseas markets has also contributed to the deceleration in activity by limiting export growth. In the first two months, heavy industry drove a drop in industrial production growth to 11.4% y/y, a two and a half year low. **Official figures that strip out the** **seasonal fluctuations in output show that three month on three month growth fell to 8.8% annualised in February from 10.1% in the prior three months.** These figures have a short history and as such are relatively untested, but they accord with anecdotal evidence that the CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly April 2012 – Appendix A 109 economy continued to lose momentum in the early part of the year. **The residential real estate** **sector is at the heart of the weakness, undermining demand for building materials. Growth in housing starts this year is down to zero as sales have plunged by 16% y/y, by a 24.3% slump in the East while the rest of the country is less badly affected (Central +1.8%, West -4.9%).** This disparity is reflected in the chart above. ###### **Inflation is now back to more comfortable levels having dropped to an average of 3.9% in** **January and February** (we average the two months to smooth out CNY distortions) and, in the absence of food or oil price shocks, we forecast it to drop below 3% in the second quarter and to slow further in the July-September period. Against the background of moderating price pressures the government has announced an unchanged inflation target of 4% for this year. This target is not binding, as is that of the ECB, for example, and policy makers will not be obliged to relax policy in order to meet it, but it does highlight the scope for easing policy. At this month’s NPC **the government signalled a modestly expansionary fiscal policy** focused on improving people’s livelihoods via expanding the social safety net, improving the provision of health care and education, and building more social housing. **Indeed, social housing received the largest budget increase, of 23%, which is aimed at supporting the completion of over 5 m social housing units this year, up from 4.3 m in 2011.** **Monetary policy is also being gradually eased** . The late February Required Reserve Ratio (RRR) cut is a high profile action, but the central bank has also boosted money market liquidity via its bill t

ransactions.  Together these operations have caused 7-day money market interest rates to drop to 3%, their lowest since the first half of 2011.  Interest rates in the real economy have also become cheaper, with discounted bills now yielding less than 6% after briefly peaking at around 12% in September. **There is even some ‘fine tuning’ of policy towards real estate.** First time buyers are being singled out for preferential access to mortgages, while China’s four largest banks are to make more funds available for developers of ‘mass market’ properties. **With Premier Wen’s reiteration that restrictive housing policies will remain in place, though, it is clear that there will be no let up in the squeeze on high-end properties and ‘speculators’.** 

**China registered a trade deficit of $31.5 bn in February, the largest single month deficit on record** .  However, CNY distortions are again important and summing the first two months of the year results in a much more modest shortfall of $4.3 bn.  The start of the year is seasonally weakest for China’s trade position and last year the same period saw a deficit of $2.0 bn, before recording a full year surplus of $156 bn.  A similar rebound is likely this year, and may have been foreshadowed by the improvement in the export order sub-index in the official PMI, from 46.9 in January to 51.1. **That has not stopped Chinese officials from suggesting that the RMB may now be close to its equilibrium value. ###### 3. Alternative scenarios: oil shock 

**The benchmark Brent oil price has risen sharply through the first quarter,** from an average around $110/bbl in the final quarter of 2011, to a recent spot record of $127/bbl, and a range around $125/bbl.  In euro terms it’s at all time highs already. 

**It’s been driven up partly by non-Opec supply difficulties, and partly by rising political tensions in the Gulf.** When prices were last at this level in the first half of 2011, in the wake of the Arab Spring, they contributed to the deceleration in the second half of the year.  Thus there is reason to think that a renewed burst of energy price inflation may stunt growth. 

Although Saudi Arabia is taking steps to defuse the market, which it appears to equate with returning the price to around $100/bbl, **further supply disruptions could easily cause the risk premium to rise further a

nd drive prices up to $150/bbl.** More ominously, an **outbreak of hostilities, for example between Iran, and Israel and the USA, could readily cause prices to surge to $200/bbl** . In both cases the real economy would pay a price. Our alternative scenarios examine the impact of oil rising to $150/bbl and to $200/bbl, although beyond the shock we allow the price of oil to revert towards a more fundamentally determined value, as the consequences of demand destruction emerge. As the adjacent table shows, **the effect of another $25/bbl increase in the price of Brent would be relatively moderate.** Our simulation suggests that growth would decelerate by 10-20 bp in 2012, and by 40-50 bp in 2013, although we have made no assumptions about collateral damage to confidence, and the effect that might have on savings rates and financial markets. As prices begin to revert to their trend path from 2014, however, growth would get a moderate 1020 bp fillip. **If prices rose to $200/bbl, however, the consequences would be much more severe.** Growth in 2013 in particular would be almost 1 percentage point lower than in our base case. **The Eurozone in particular would endure another year of outright contraction,** and China would experience a second year of deceleration following 2012. The USA would be driven perilously close to recession itself. The resultant demand destruction would weaken oil prices significantly in the aftermath of the shock, however. That could be worth 40 bp on the growth rate in 2014 and 2015, although the output lost might not be made up in full until 2016 or 2017. Registrations in Italy, for example, were almost as weak as they were in France, and fell 19% y/y. **In fact, demand for new cars fell in all major economies except Germany – the only major market not to decline.** In terms of production, motor vehicle output surged in the UK but not so much elsewhere. According to Vauxhall Motors, European car manufacturers are suffering from unsustainable

overcapacity. **Honda, meanwhile, plans to double its production of cars in Europe as it seeks to reduce reliance on Japanese imports and exposure to the appreciation of the yen** . The outlook for this year remains bleak as tough austerity measures are expected to drive down demand. As a consequence of our outlook for the Eurozone, we forecast another difficult couple of years ahead for the European motor vehicle sector with output set to contract in 2012 and 2013, and staging a very moderate recovery beyond then. ###### **4.1.3 Asia** **The decline in global auto registrations since the start of 2012 has been mostly driven by a drop in Chinese registrations** . Registrations fell 10.6% m/m in January while production declined 8.3%. Nevertheless, we expect growth to pick up and for China to be an almost 20 million vehicle market in 2012. **Some of the decline in China was offset in other parts of Asia, with gains in India (21.6% m/m) and Japan (14.2 m/m).** Japanese brands had a better supply of vehicles after recovering from production disruptions caused by the earthquake in Japan and flooding in Thailand. Our outlook for Japan is that production will remain around the 2010 mark until at least 2016 because of lacklustre domestic demand and because of plans for firms to relocate output to weaker currency areas, including the USA, as Japan hollows out its auto industry further. %). Construction spending decreased most sharply in the Czech Republic where it fell over 20% m/m in January.

In March, there was no growth in housing starts as sales plunged by 16% y/y, due to a 24.3% slump in the East while the rest of the country was less badly affected. Overall house building is forecast to continue to grow this year, albeit at a slower rate than in 2011. 

**In Japan, the construction index fell almost 2% in December, but construction orders placed the following month increased by 24.6% y/y.** We expect there to be some gains in output generated by reconstruction activity after the Japanese tsunami.

###### 1. Company mergers and acquisitions 

###### **KGHM acquires Quadra FNX** 

- On 25<sup>th</sup> January, the **Polish treasury ministry** announced that it would “thoroughly analyse” **KGHM** ’s proposed acquisition of Quadra FNX. As the government owns a 32% stake in KGHM, this raised the prospects that it could move to block the deal.  In the previous week, the government had blocked a proposed 3 billion zloty (US$884.7 million) share buyback by KGHM. 

- On 5<sup>th</sup> March, it was reported that **KGHM** had completed the planned takeover of the **Quadra FNX Mining** in a deal worth US$2.91B after it was approved by the Quadra stakeholders. KGHM Chief Executive Officer announced that the Polish miner is eying additional acquisitions as part of a strategy to reach an

annual output of 700,000t by 2018. 

###### **Minmetals Resources acquires Anvil Mining** 

- **Minmetals Resources** ( **MMR** ) announced the acquisition of over 90% of **Anvil Mining** shares on 17<sup>th</sup> February, through its US$1.3B bid for the company.  The remaining shares will now be compulsorily acquired. MMR, which is 72% owned by China’s **Minmetals Group** ( **MMG** ), has operating copper assets in Laos and Australia and now adds Anvil’s 60,000t/y **Kinsevere** SXEW mine in DR Congo to its portfolio. 

###### **Xstrata eyeing Glencore merger** 

- The proposed merger between **Glencore** , the world’s largest commodity trading company, and **Xstrata** is set to go through in a deal worth US$39 Billion, according to a joint statement released by the companies on 7<sup>th</sup> February.  The deal, described as an ‘all share merger of equals’, would see Glencore offering 2.8 new shares for each Xstrata share, equivalent to a 15.2% premium.  This would give Glencore shareholders a controlling share of 56% in the US$90B merged company called **Glencore Xstrata International,** with the remaining 44% owned by Xstrata shareholders.  The deal has yet to receive approval from Xstrata shareholders.  Although Glencore has traditionally focused on commodity trading, the company has become increasingly involved in the mining stage of the supply chain through recent acquisitions.  The new company would be a fully integrated commodity supplier with mining, processing, logistics and marketing.  Currently, Glencore owns a 34% stake in Xstrata.  Xstrata is one of the world’s leading copper mining companies whose assets include the 64,000t/y copper-in-concentrate **Ernest Henry** and 166,000t/y **Mount Isa** mines in Australia as well as equity stakes in the South American operations **Alumbrera** (131,000t/y), **Collahuasi** (433,000t/y) and **Antamina** (396,000t/y). 

- The proposed merger between **Glencore** and **Xstrata** is set to undergo scrutiny by the European Antitrust Commission, according to a statement released by the companies on 24<sup>th</sup> February.  This is only the first of a number of regulatory antitrust hurdles that need to be cleared before the merger can go through.  Similar processes are expected in the US and China.

###### **Electricity** 

- The Zambian state power company, **Zesco Ltd** ., announced on 25<sup>th</sup> January that it plans to raise electricity prices by 17-33% from May in order to raise funds for re-investment in the electricity sector.  The company also said that the power sector had recently been experiencing higher costs as costs of inputs have increased due to the increase in commodity prices and depreciation of the Zambian Kwacha. ###### **Kansanshi** 

- Production at the **Kansanshi** Mine in Zambia ground to a halt as workers began a strike on 1<sup>st</sup> March, demanding a 17% pay rise. On March 4<sup>th</sup> the management and the workers agreed to a 15% pay rise, but a settlement has not yet been reached on the duration of the new contract. Nevertheless, workers returned to work on 6<sup>th</sup> March. This is the second strike at the mine this year. In 2012, the mine is expected to produce 144,000t of copper-in-concentrate. 

- On 16<sup>th</sup> March, it was reported that the talks over a new labour contract between the management and workers at **First Quantum Minerals** ’ **Kansanshi** mine in Zambia had collapsed and were set to be resolved in an industrial relations court. 

###### **Mopani Mines** 

- On 28<sup>th</sup> January, 3,000 workers at **Glencore** ’s **Mopani Mines** in Zambia staged a 12-hour strike after they were offered a 12% pay rise instead of the 20% increase which they were demanding. Subsequently, on 2<sup>nd</sup> February the **Mineworkers Union of Zambia** and the **National Union of Mine and Allied Workers** reached an agreement with the Mopani Copper Mines management on a 17% pay rise.  This news comes shortly after striking workers at the **Kansanshi** mine were awarded an equivalent pay rise. Mopani Copper Mines operates the **Mufulira** and **Nkana** copper mines in Zambia with an estimated combined production 92,000t of copper-in-concentrate in 2012. 

- On 1<sup>st</sup> March, the **Zambian Environmental Management Agency** (ZEMA) ordered **Glencore** ’s **Mopani Copper Mines** to shut down its **Mufulira** heap leaching plant due to pollution violations. The agency suspects that the emissions of acid mist have caused an increase in pulmonary, throat, nose and ear ailments in the surrounding area.  Mopani copper mines subsequently announced that it will spend US$145M on an anti-pollution programme over the next two years.  The Mopani Copper Mines heap leaching plant is expected to produce 6,000t of EW cathode in 2012.

- In a statement by **Codelco** on 6<sup>th</sup> March, the company announced plans to invest US$4.33B in its Chilean mines in 2012. This is a substantial increase from the US$2.5B the company spent in 2011. This is part of a strategy to counteract declining output levels and boost output to 2.1Mt of refined copper by 2020. 

###### **Collahuasi** 

- Operations were halted at the **Collahuasi** mine in Chile during 20-21 February, following the death of a worker at the associated sulphide plant.  The mine’s management did not reveal what impact the stoppage would have on output.  We currently expect the Collahuasi mine to produce 433,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 28,000t of EW cathode in 2012. 

###### **Earthquake** 

- Central Chile was hit by a 7.1 magnitude earthquake on 25<sup>th</sup> March.  However, no casualties were reported and there was no serious damage to infrastructure.  There are several major copper mines near the epicentre of the earthquake, including **Codelcos Andina** and **El Teniente** and Anglo **American** ’s **Los Bronces** .  However, operations at the mines were reported to be normal.  This is the largest earthquake to hit Chile since the 8.8 magnitude tremor in 2010 that caused 500 fatalities and major destruction. 

###### **Escondida** 

- **BHP Billiton** announced plans on 14<sup>th</sup> February to develop a new 152,000t/d concentrator plant at the **Escondida** mine in Chile to replace the **Los Colorados** concentrator.  The project will cost US$3.8B and is expected to be commissioned in H1 2015.  This development is part of BHP Billiton’s strategy aimed at increasing contained copper production capacity at Escondida to 1.3Mt/y by 2015-2016. 

###### **Floods** 

- Heavy rains in the region of Calama, in Chile’s Atacama Desert, halted production at a number of mines on Sunday 12<sup>th</sup> February, mainly for safety reasons. The majority had returned to normal operations by Tuesday 14<sup>th</sup> , however, as the hazardous weather retreated.  The affected mines include the **Chuquicamata** , **Radomiro Tom

ic** , **El Abra** and **Gaby** and the **Ministro Hales** project. Nearby mines **Spence** , **El Tesoro** and **Esperanza** did not report any disruptions to production. 

- Heavy rains in **Northern Chile** have continued to affect the operations of several major mines in the area.  On 13<sup>th</sup> March, it was reported that the **Haldeman Mining Company** , owners of the **Sagasca** mine, had declared _force majeure_ , following mudslides disrupting operations.  Furthermore, access roads to the **Collahuasi** and **Cerro Colorado** mines became impassable due to flooding and there have been unconfirmed reports of direct flooding on the grounds of the Collahuasi mine itself. Nevertheless, it was reported that operations have continued. 

###### **2.5.2 Peru** 

###### **Quellaveco** 

- **Mitsubishi Corp** announced on 17<sup>th</sup> February the acquisition of 18.1% of the copper project **Quellaveco** (Peru) from the **International Finance Corporation** .  The remaining 81.9% belongs to **Anglo American** , which treats Quellaveco as a high priority amongst its list of projects to develop.  It is estimated that Quellaveco requires an investment of US$3.2B and is set to produce around 225,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate.

###### 3. Smelter production 

###### 3.1 Africa 

###### **3.1.1 Tanzania** 

###### **Danformation** 

- On 26<sup>th</sup> March, it was announced that Tanzania’s first copper smelter operated by **Danformation** is due to start operations within a few days with the arrival of first consignment of ore.  The smelter has already been commissioned and currently has a capacity of 12,000-18,000t/y of copper-in-blister that will gradually be expanded to 240,000t/y.  This is the first of six smelters that Danformation plans to build in Tanzania. 

###### 3.2 Asia 

###### **3.2.1 China** 

###### **Longyan City** 

- On 25<sup>th</sup> January, production at **Zijin Mining Group** ’s smelting project in **Longyan City, Fujian province** in China was suspended for investigation after three workers died in an industrial accident. The smelter had recently started trial production that was scheduled to run until 15<sup>th</sup> June 2012.  The plant has a full capacity of 200,000t/y but had been operating at low levels during the trial period 

###### **3.2.2 India** 

###### **Sterlite Industries’ Tuticorin** 

- Following an environmental inspection, on 21<sup>st</sup> October 2011 the supreme court of India instructed **Sterlite Industries** ’ **Tuticorin** copper smelter to reduce its level of environmental pollution.  The **Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board** ( **TNPCB** ) has been tasked with issuing directions to the smelter on how to reduce its levels of pollution.  The TNPCB is also responsible for setting a reasonable timeframe for the smelter to undertake changes.  In 2011, Tuticorin is expected to produce 295,000t of copper

blister. 

###### **3.2.3 Japan** 

###### **Saganoseki** 

- **Pan Pacific Copper Co.** suspended operations at its **Saganoseki** smelter in the southern province of Oita, Japan after high voltage cabling and an electric power substation were damaged due to fire on 7<sup>th</sup> January.  In 2011, the smelter produced  235,000t of copper cathode (this does not include the copper anode produced for off-site refining). The smelter resumed operations on 13<sup>th</sup> February. It is estimated that the plant incurred a 30,000t loss in production as a result of the shutdown, however, deliveries are said to have remained unaffected due to high stocks of anode. 

###### **Tamano** 

- **Pan Pacific Copper** is also reported to be experiencing production problems at the **Tamano** smelter (operated by **Hibi Kyodo** ). According to reports, a malfunctioning boiler caused the smelter to shut down during 6<sup>th</sup> -21<sup>st</sup> February. 

###### **3.2.4 Kazakhstan** 

###### **AO Kazzinc** 

- **AO Kazzinc** , a subsidiary of **Glencore International Plc.** , announced on 16<sup>th</sup> September the 

commissioning of its copper smelting and refining project in Ust-Kamenogorsk, Eastern Kazakhstan.

The plant currently has a production capacity of 70,000t/y, and there is potential for this figure to rise by a further 17,500t/y in the future. 

###### **3.2.5 Philippines** 

###### **Leyte** 

- On 20<sup>th</sup> March, the management of **PASAR** ’s **Leyte** smelter in the Philippines, majority owned by **Glencore** , announced that the smelter is expected to resume operations in June or July. This comes after operations were halted in January following a fire.  PASAR’s spokesman explained that the fire had damaged the anti-pollution devices (i.e. the sulphuric acid plant) at the smelter and new equipment had been ordered from China. He said that the smelter is technically operational but cannot operate without anti-pollution devices due to the Philippine environmental regulation. No estimates were given of the expected production losses from the six-month shutdown. The PASAR smelter has an annual capacity of 210,000t copper-in-blister. 

###### 3.3 South and Central America 

###### **3.3.1 Chile** 

###### **Charges** 

- On 6<sup>th</sup> February, it was reported that operations had been halted at **Anglo American** ’s 140,000t/y **Chagres** smelter in Chile after subcontractors staged a labour strike.  The workers’ union of the subcontractor Tranex, a company working with transport of concentrates and ores, blocked the access to the smelter, claiming that Anglo American was restricting the right of the workers to unionize.  The strike was also endorsed by the president of Chile’s **Confederation of Copper Workers** (CTC). 

###### **Chuquicamata** 

- On 19<sup>th</sup> March, it was reported that **Codelco** had restarted the **Chuquicamata**

smelter in Northern Chile after production had been halted for a month due to a blocked chimney.  The smelter is expected to produce 360,000t copper-in-blister in 2012. 

###### **3.3.2 Peru** 

###### **La Oroya** 

- The government of Peru has supported plans to restart **Doe Run Peru** ’s 75,000t/y **La Oroya** smelter. The restart is expected on 1<sup>st</sup> May 2012, subject to Peru’s congress approving a bill for the extension of a clean-up programme at the plant.  The clean-up, which entails cutting back sulphur dioxide emissions, is over half-way complete, however, it requires another US$168M of investment to finalise.  The plant has remained shut since June 2009 as a result of financial difficulties caused by the financial crisis.  Upon reopening, the plant’s operators hope to embark on a US$200M expansion plan, which will be financed by **Glencore** (US$135) and the **Renco Group** (US$65M). **Glencore** is said to supply most of the concentrates, with the rest coming from small and medium-sized local mines.

# Appendix D Production forecasting methodology and guide to Chapter 2 & Appendix C tables 

The basis for our forecasts of mine, smelter and refinery production is the CRU Copper Raw Materials Database (CuRMat), which contains operational data for mines, smelters and refineries.  The data are shown in Appendix C, on an operation by operation basis.  These include historical production and planned production at existing operations under ideal operating conditions.  Our detailed table of projects is also included in Appendix C.  The start up year is based on company projections together with CRU’s view on what is technically feasible in the time period allowed. 

###### Operations and projects 

To arrive at our forecasts, firstly we consider planned production from committed operations. This includes all existing operations and projects that are definitely going ahead (ie those that fall into our “firm” category, see below for project definitions) less any planned closures. 

All projects are classified as “firm”, “probable” or “possible” according to the likelihood of them being developed during our five year forecast horizon.  In the short term, this depends on the stage of development of the projects.  The definitions of “firm”, “probable” and “possible” are: 

**Firm** Projects where permitting has been successfully completed and financing is well underway.  Construction may already have started.  Except for unforeseen disasters, these projects should be operating in the very near future, within a maximum of 2-4 years.  It should also be noted that, although these projects are in the final

stages, they might very well be held up by other unforeseen factors such as political instability or sharp falls in the metals prices. 

**Probable** Projects for which the full or bankable feasibility study has started or is well underway and a successful outcome is expected. 

CRU International Limited confidential 

Copper Quarterly April 2012 Appendix D 

232 

**Possible** Feasibility studies have started or are about to start, and there are indications that the economics of the project appear sound.  However, it is not a foregone conclusion at this point that the project will or will not advance to further stages. 

Projects are then classified further according to the type of development, ie greenfield project, brownfield expansion or extension, restart or redevelopment.  There are also a few projects classified as brownfield projects.  This involves the development of a new resource, for example a sulphide orebody at an SXEW operation or the exploitation of a tailings dump at a site where there is already some equipment or infrastructure. 

Firm brownfield expansions and extensions are incorporated into the production figures for the operation and therefore included in the mine-by-mine and country-by-country figures, along with the existing operations.  Restarts at mines which have been closed for less than five years are also included in these figures.  These projects are given a 100% probability of going ahead. However, they are subject to the same standard disruption allowance (see below) as all existing operations. 

Greenfield projects and redevelopments are not included in these figures, due to the higher risks of delays or technical problems.  These projects have been given a 90% probability of going ahead.  These numbers appear in our tables as “committed projects” and the global total is added to the global total (before disruption) for existing operations.  These figures are then subject to the standard disruption allowance. 

A probability factor is applied to the total production that would be expected from probable and possible projects if they are brought on stream.  Probable projects are given a 70% probability of going ahead and the possible projects a 40% probability.  These figures are then subject to the standard disruption allowance. 

###### Disruption allowance 

A disruption allowance is applied to mine production to allow for unforeseen problems, such as strikes, ore grades, adverse weather conditions, earthquakes, technological problems etc.  This disruption allowance is not specific to a particular set of operations; rather it is applied to the industry as a whole based on CRU’s experience. The disruption allowance is independent from any market condition and simply reflects the general production performance of the industry. 

###### Market adjustment 

A bottom line market adjustment is applied whenever we consider that this is justified by market conditions.  Such an adjustment was applied in previous Copper

Quarterly Reports because we considered that mine cuts would be necessary to balance the refined copper market., and indeed would occur in response to low prices.  However, our consumption forecasts have been revised upwards and we are no longer forecasting that prices will fall below the mine cost curve.  We have removed the market adjustment for mines since our Copper Quarterly October 2009 production forecast. 

The same methodology is applied to smelter and refined output.  In addition, we apply a market adjustment to smelter and refined production to take account of raw material shortages.  This is made after we have considered a reaction to the markets for refined copper and sulphuric acid. As concentrate stocks are now estimated to be critically low, smelter output is lowered to

balance the concentrates market.  Refined production then needs to be reduced to balance the blister market. 

The figures presented in the tables in Chapter 2 and Appendix C represent different stages in the forecasting process. **Table 2.1** summarises our forecasts and indicates the process flow from mines to refined copper by each of the process routes.  The following paragraphs explain how the figures in the remaining tables in Chapter 2 are arrived at.  In all tables, the figures for 2011 and all preceding years are actual figures, based on reported numbers.  Those from 2012 onwards are forecasts. 

###### 1.  Mine supply and raw materials for smelting 

**Table 2.2** shows our figures (historical and forecasted) of mine production by copper product, and how these are arrived at.  For copper concentrates and EW mines it shows committed production (from existing operations and committed projects) before and after disruption, the market related adjustment; and our forecasts of production from probable and possible projects. For other concentrates and cement the figures shown are after disruption.  No market adjustments are applied to these figures.  These are our final forecast figures. 

The concentrates and other raw materials for smelting shown in **table 2.2** includes copper in copper concentrates, the copper in copper/nickel concentrates produced by Vale Inco and Norilsk (treated via the copper smelter and refinery route), a portion of the copper in other concentrates and copper in cement.  Other copper/nickel concentrates are treated via the nickel route and a copper matte produced that is then refined by electrowinning.  The figures are derived from the output by these two producers adjusted by our standard disruption allowance. 

**Table 2.3** presents the copper labour contract expiry dates from 2012. 

Two new tables were added in the July 2011 Quarterly report.  In **Table 2.4** we summarise production from projects by status (firm, probable and possible) both before and after the probabilities have been applied. **Table 2.5** provides a list of all firm projec

ts due on stream in 2011 with year by year production. 

**Tables 2.6 and 2.7** show regional committed mine production (historical and forecasted) by country and by product, respectively.  This is production from all existing mines and all committed projects.  The detailed figures in the breakdowns by country and by product are before the disruption allowance that is applied to the bottom line global figure. 

In **Appendix C.2** , we now also list all projects (firm, probable and possible) due on stream over the forecast period with year-by-year production from each project, before any adjustment for either project risk or disruptions.  Thus, the total reflects potential output from all mine projects. 

###### 2.  Smelter production 

**Table 2.8** shows the calculations to arrive at our final smelter production figures (historical and forecast), including all adjustments.  We show committed output before and after the disruption allowance, plus the forecast output from probable and possible projects.  As with mines, this is a proportion of potential new output from projects that are not classified as committed.  We then apply, if necessary, additional market adjustments for a reaction to the refined copper and sulphuric acid markets as well as to balance the concentrates market.  In this Copper Quarterly

Report, we have only included an adjustment due to raw material availability as the pressures on the uptake of sulphuric acid are now over. 

Committed smelter output by country is shown in **table 2.10** .  The figures show the level of output that we believe could be achieved by existing operations and by committed new capacity (firm smelter projects), under the assumption that sufficient raw materials are available.  The disruption allowance is applied to the bottom line global figure. 

###### 3.  Refined copper production 

Our production figures (historical and forecast) of refined copper production and how we arrive at these are shown in **table 2.9** .  Output is shown by process of raw materials.  Primary output in the total electro/fire refined production is the final outcome that originates from concentrates. Secondary output refers to production from scrap, either via smelting or anode casting. Electrowon includes conventional EW from oxide concentrates, as well as EW from sulphide concentrates and RLE output also from concentrates. 

The table shows committed output for electro-refined, fire-refined, conventional EW, EW/RLE from concentrates and NiCuEW.  Each output is considered before and after the disruption allowance.  The committed output will correspond to that in tables 2.11 and 2.12.  Then the forecast output from probable and possible projects is added.  As for mines and smelters, this is a proportion of potential new output from projects that are not classified as committed.  For electrorefined output we then apply additional market

adjustments for a reaction to the refined copper market and to balance the blister market.  An additional market adjustment is also applied to EW output corresponding to the adjustment made to mine production. 

**Tables 2.11 and 2.12** show committed refined copper production by country and by process, respectively.  This is production from all existing operations and all committed projects.  The detailed figures in the breakdowns by country and by product are before disruption allowance, which is applied to the bottom line global figure. 

###### 4.  The raw materials balance tables 

**Table 2.13** shows the balance in copper in concentrates and other raw materials. 

The first half of the table (sections A and B) shows the potential shortfall in concentrates for smelting. 

**Section A** accounts for the mine supply of raw materials for smelting.  This has already been described above in section 1. 

**Section B** shows smelter demand, i.e. smelter requirements under ideal operating conditions with no restrictions.  However, the standard disruption allowance has been applied to smelter requirements, and also may include a market adjustment to account for a response to low copper prices, refined copper demand and sulphuric acid demand, where necessary. 

The first line in section B shows potential smelter output.  This is the sum of the committed, probable and possible figures in table 2.8.  Our assumed loss from cutbacks due to low prices is then subtracted.  Production of EW and RLE refined copper from concentrates is also added, since this is an addition to concentrate demand.

**Section C** is the balance between mine supply and smelter demand.  This shows a large shortfall all through our 5-year forecast period. 

The second half of the table shows our forecast balance after all adjustments. 

**Section D** shows our assumptions of cutbacks necessary to bring the market back into balance, which correspond to table 2.8. 

**Section E** then shows our forecasts of smelter production and concentrates requirements. Smelter production corresponds with the figure in table 2.8. 

**Table 2.14** shows the blister balance.  This follows the same layout and methodology as table 2.13.  The first part of the table shows the potential balance based on planned refined copper output.
